\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
$K{\geq}3$ multi-method consensus reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 conditions with known consensus (Padding-410M and Pythia-1.4B C4 pending audit), confirming that multi-method agreement generalizes beyond the calibration setup; Pythia-1.4B (s42: 1/8, s43: 3/8) and SmolLM3-3B (3/8) reflect scale-dependent seed sensitivity and canary metric splitting rather than framework failure.
Reverse-direction tests at $\alpha{=}1.0$ reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence at full synthetic replacement), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
The unidirectionality of token entropy is domain-dependent: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4 (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling absent from all WikiText conditions at any contamination level (see below).
GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance, placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (consistent with the null regime) and moderate detection (3--4/8) only at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to method recommendation.}
The primary value of the multi-method framework is not the consensus vote itself but the systematic comparison it enables.
By applying five methods with different inductive biases to the same data, the framework reveals \emph{why} each method succeeds or fails: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR because it captures reverse-directional associations; differenced cross-correlation cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence; threshold onset lacks power at $T{=}11$ under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}); and Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8) but remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
This process of elimination converges on permutation Granger as the recommended method: it is the only one combining zero null-control FPR, consistent detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$, and clean directional separation on WikiText (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution, maintaining FPR${=}$0\%; however, the practical recommendation is simpler: for short iterative training series, permutation Granger alone provides reliable detection without requiring the full consensus machinery.
Multi-method consensus ($K{\geq}3$) remains useful as a robustness check, reaching ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 cross-architecture conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), but threshold onset is power-limited and Toda--Yamamoto provides moderate supplementary signal (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with four contributing methods supporting the $K{\geq}3$ threshold.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
After correcting a statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), confirming that its lower rates reflect genuine power limitations at $T{=}11$ rather than implementation error.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
After implementation correction, Toda--Yamamoto's window sensitivity is consistent with its moderate detection profile: TY consensus stabilizes at $T{\geq}6$, slightly later than the primary methods ($T{\geq}5$), reflecting the additional degrees of freedom consumed by the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{Four-layer detection taxonomy.}
Our results suggest a layered taxonomy for detecting iterative training degradation, ordered by onset threshold:
(1)~\emph{Distributional dimensionality} (effective rank): detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom, with onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.10$ (established);
(2)~\emph{Distributional instability} (entropy variance): detects inflated fluctuations in canary metrics across generations, with suggestive onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$ (a $10\times$ variance inflation from $0.004$ to $0.04$), well before causal coupling emerges;
(3)~\emph{Causal coupling} (Granger-type tests): detects temporal precedence between canary and downstream metrics, with onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ (the detection phase transition established in \S\ref{sec:regime}); and
(4)~\emph{Dynamical stability} (AC1): suggestive evidence of autocorrelation shifts near the onset boundary (see below), but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$.
Layers~1 and~3 are established; Layers~2 and~4 are suggestive and require longer generation protocols for confirmation ($T{\geq}50$; \citealt{dakos2012methods}).
These four layers are complementary rather than redundant.
Distributional anomalies (effective rank, Layer~1) emerge at $\alpha{\geq}0.10$, while causal detectability (PermG, Layer~3) requires $\alpha{\geq}0.50$---a 40-percentage-point gap between structural distortion and causal evidence.
This gap constitutes the detection phase transition: collapse is visible long before it becomes causally traceable, and the layers can diverge across architectures.

\paragraph{Suggestive CSD signatures.}
Exploratory analysis reveals a CSD-consistent pattern: canary metrics show rising autocorrelation (Kendall $\tau{=}0.79$--$0.82$, $p{<}0.001$) while downstream diversity metrics show none ($\tau{=}0.03$--$0.30$, $p{>}0.19$), suggestive of a temporal sequence in which canary destabilization precedes downstream collapse.
However, this dissociation does not survive multiple testing correction (2/10 conditions significant post-BH), and surrogate-based validation would be needed to confirm CSD against colored-noise alternatives~\cite{dakos2012methods}.
$T{=}20$ replication may strengthen this evidence; at $T{=}11$ the 95\% confidence interval for AC1 is approximately $\pm 0.3$, precluding confirmatory claims~\cite{scheffer2009early}.

\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
As a distributional dimensionality indicator, effective rank tracks contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom---Layer~1 in the taxonomy above.
However, effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines---a limitation specific to the dimensionality layer that does not affect the causal coupling layer (Granger detectability), which remains consistent across architectures.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method analysis: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}
The non-monotonic dose-response at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (PermG fwd: s42 3/8, s43 0/8, below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $\alpha{=}0.75$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) is consistent with the $S \times R$ prediction in \S\ref{sec:theory}: at $\alpha{=}0.60$, relaxation time matching drives temporal resolution $R \to 0$---entropy and diversity respond within the same generation---so that despite increasing signal strength $S$, the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
At lower contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $R$ remains high---entropy leads diversity by a full generation---and $S$ has just crossed the detection threshold, yielding sufficient $S \times R$.
At higher contamination ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), $S$ grows large enough to dominate: entropy collapses within generation~0$\to$1 while diversity still requires generation~1$\to$2, restoring $R$ and driving $S \times R$ well above the detection floor.
The synchronous dip is mechanistically distinct from the blind regime: in the blind regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$), canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous dip, both metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
This creates a four-regime structure---blind, onset, synchronous dip, detection---rather than the two-regime detect/no-detect boundary assumed by simpler models.
Toda--Yamamoto maintains moderate detection (3--4/8) across the $\alpha{=}0.50$--$0.75$ range including the synchronous zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8, suggesting partial inter-method complementarity: TY's augmented VAR formulation may be less sensitive to the temporal synchronization that suppresses PermG's signal at $\alpha{=}0.60$.
The finding also has practical implications: simple threshold-based triggers (e.g., the 15\% entropy criterion) fire at $\alpha{=}0.60$ because they respond to magnitude rather than temporal structure, suggesting that threshold triggers may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
The unidirectional forward causation observed consistently in WikiText experiments (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all contamination levels and seeds) does not hold universally.
On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Pythia-410M, s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8 (forward: 8/8), indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling between canary and downstream metrics (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
This stands in sharp contrast to the same model at the same contamination level on WikiText, where PermG reverse${=}$0/8.
One possible explanation is that C4's broader distributional characteristics (Common Crawl vs.\ encyclopedic Wikipedia text) alter the temporal dynamics of collapse: the richer distributional structure may allow downstream diversity metrics to feed back into canary metrics more quickly, shortening the temporal offset that WikiText's narrower distribution preserves.
Alternatively, the pre-training data confound (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) may play a role, since Pythia was pre-trained on the Pile which includes C4-overlapping data.
The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain rather than assumed to transfer from WikiText-based calibration; the forward detection itself (PermG fwd${=}$8/8) remains robust across both domains.

\paragraph{Canary metric choice as a sensitivity dimension.}
SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a dimension of method sensitivity beyond the five statistical methods analyzed in Claim~3.
Token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations in SmolLM3, violating the monotonic decline assumed by Granger tests and producing 0/4 significant entropy$\to$downstream pairs.
ECE, by contrast, maintains monotonic growth and achieves 3/4 significant pairs (PermG fwd: 3/8 overall).
The two canary types activate through partially disjoint method subsets: entropy pairs reach significance via naive and differenced cross-correlation, while ECE pairs reach significance via differenced cross-correlation and permutation Granger.
SmolLM3-3B achieves $K{\geq}3$ = 3/8 (matching PermG fwd), confirming that consensus tracks individual-method detection even in this challenging case; however, the low overall detection (3/8) places SmolLM3 as one of three outliers ($K{\geq}3$ $<6/8$) across the 14-condition cross-architecture panel.
This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal.
The practical implication is that monitoring dashboards should track multiple canary candidates, adapting the active metric to the architecture under evaluation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.45$, where early warning would be most valuable, aggregate canary detection remains null (a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ but does not reach aggregate detection through $\alpha{=}0.45$).
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.

\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), validated across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, provide cross-scale evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.

\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the scope of intervention validation (three seed-precision pairs across two model scales at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment---particularly to larger models and accumulate-mode training---requires further confirmation.
The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; notably, the threshold trigger fires at $\alpha{=}0.60$ even though formal Granger detection fails at this level (synchronous collapse zone; \S\ref{sec:regime}), illustrating that magnitude-based triggers can complement temporal-precedence tests.
However, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods; Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection (3--4/8) at $T{=}11$ reflects this constraint, as the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ consumes additional degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.

Change-point analysis under the null condition ($\alpha{=}0.00$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary$\to$downstream significance (24/24) while eliminating reverse-direction signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Multi-seed replication across the six validated architecture families would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}7$B parameters) remains an open direction.
Longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$ generations) could unlock threshold onset detection, which requires more generation-over-generation differences for $3\sigma$ calibration to achieve adequate power; longer runs could also improve Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection rates by providing additional degrees of freedom for the augmented VAR (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
The SmolLM3 finding (ECE-only detection due to non-monotonic entropy) motivates systematic study of which canary metric is most reliable per architecture family.
Online monitoring, where canary metrics are computed within training pipelines for real-time collapse detection, is a natural applied extension.
Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
The sigmoid quantification of the onset boundary ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) invites connection to theoretical frameworks---the critical mixture ratio scaling law of \citet{gu2024cmr}, the data-mixing phase transitions of \citet{gu2025datamixing}, and the universality classes of \citet{truong2025entropy}---that could explain why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime and whether the non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ reflects a transition boundary; these connections remain speculative and require finer $\alpha$ resolution to validate.

\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ at $T{=}10$, steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$, $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the detection phase transition is specification-invariant.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, 24/24 forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance with 0/24 reverse (4~seeds); directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).
Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable causal signal in the canary metrics.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{Metric trajectories at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds). Token entropy drops at generation~1; distinct-1 declines from generations~2--3, with a consistent one-generation canary lead across all four seeds (shaded: inter-seed range). This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant pairs.}
\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, s42: 3/8, s43: 0/8; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed across 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, forward-direction significance rates range from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 37.5\% (PermG), with inter-method $\kappa = 0.185$ (near chance) and a spurious rate of at least 62.5\%.
PermG is the only method that combines zero null-control FPR with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}); its nonparametric null distribution, built-in directionality, and hyperparameter-free design explain this advantage.
The $S \times R$ framework generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$ via $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ should left-shift, (ii)~the transition should smooth, and (iii)~different methods should exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values.
These predictions are under empirical verification.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate the detection phase transition across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B parameters, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} reports PermG forward detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}$6/8 in 13 of 15 conditions (87\%).
Two exceptions emerge: Pythia-1.4B seed~42 on WikiText (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43, and SmolLM3-3B (3/8), where only ECE$\to$downstream pairs reach significance while entropy$\to$downstream pairs fail entirely (0/4; details in Appendix).
SmolLM3's token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations; this pattern violates the monotonic decline that Granger tests require.
The onset boundary $\alpha_c \approx 0.50$ at $T{=}10$ is architecture-independent: every family that achieves detection does so at or above this threshold, and none achieves reliable detection below it.

Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest detection observed: Pythia-1B reaches PermG~fwd 8/8 (2~seeds), and Pythia-1.4B reaches 8/8 on C4 versus 2/8 on WikiText at the same scale.
At Pythia-6.9B (bf16), detection recovers to 7/8 on WikiText.
Dataset characteristics modulate detection power independently of model capacity.
Directional asymmetry also varies by domain: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4, PermG reverse reaches 7/8, compared to 0/24 across all WikiText conditions.
This domain-dependent bidirectionality suggests that the unidirectional forward causation observed on WikiText may partly reflect domain-specific dynamics (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\subsection{Canary-Based Early Intervention}
\label{sec:intervention}

We implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ switches to $0.0$ (pure real data).
A reactive baseline triggers when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$.
The predictive trigger fires at generation~1 in both Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32), one generation before the reactive baseline (generation~2).
Peak perplexity under predictive intervention is $56.99$ versus $157.09$ under reactive (s42 fp32), a 58\% reduction (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%).
Recovery occurs at generation~2 under predictive cessation versus generation~4 under reactive.
Both models converge to the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline by generation~10.

The trigger generation, recovery timeline, and convergence behavior are identical across the $3.4\times$ scale gap from 410M to 1.4B, and the 15\% entropy threshold generalizes without recalibration.
These results position canary-based detection within a four-layer taxonomy of collapse monitoring: (1)~dimensionality collapse, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.10$ via $n$-gram diversity decline; (2)~distributional variance, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.25$ via calibration drift; (3)~causal coupling, detectable at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ via Granger precedence; and (4)~dynamical stability, assessable at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ via lag structure.
Each layer captures a distinct aspect of collapse, and lower layers activate at lower contamination thresholds.
The practical implication is that canary monitoring should combine multiple detection layers rather than rely on any single statistical test.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	The experiments in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}--\ref{sec:consensus_validation} reveal that lead-lag conclusions in iterative training collapse are fragile along multiple axes.
5	This section distills three methodological pitfalls (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}), proposes a multi-method consensus framework to quantify their impact and identify the most reliable individual method (\S\ref{sec:consensus}), and calibrates the framework's error rates using built-in experimental controls (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
6	
7	
8	\subsection{Methodological Pitfalls in Lead-Lag Analysis}
9	\label{sec:pitfalls}
10	
11	We identify three pitfalls that, individually or in combination, can produce incorrect conclusions about temporal precedence in iterative training systems.
12	Each is documented below with representative data from our experiments; full results appear in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Pitfall 1: Method sensitivity.}
15	Applied to the same data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs: 4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics, including candidates later excluded per \S\ref{sec:case_study}), five lead-lag detection methods yield FDR significance rates ranging from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 37.5\% (permutation Granger), with Toda--Yamamoto achieving moderate rates (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$); inter-method agreement is Cohen's $\kappa{=}0.185$, indicating poor agreement (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
16	The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs flagged by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is at least 62.5\% across the primary methods.
17	This pitfall is dangerous because method choice alone can determine whether a lead-lag relationship is deemed present or absent.
18	In a literature where single-method analyses are the norm, the implicit assumption that method choice does not matter is demonstrably false.
19	
20	\paragraph{Pitfall 2: Spurious regression under shared trends.}
21	A single preprocessing decision, first-differencing to remove shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}, can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
22	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, canary$\to$perplexity pairs appear near-universally significant in undifferenced analysis ($F{=}16$--$36$) but yield $F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a; \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
23	In contrast, canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24).
24	Without the differencing diagnostic, an analyst would conclude that canaries predict perplexity, a conclusion entirely driven by co-trending rather than temporal precedence.
25	The danger lies in the selective nature of this confound: only by applying the diagnostic can one determine which channels are genuine and which are artifacts of shared non-stationarity.
26	
27	\paragraph{Pitfall 3: Regime dependence.}
28	Even after fixing the statistical method, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a lead-lag relationship is detectable.
29	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH FDR-corrected at $q{=}0.05$) find 6/8 pairs FDR-significant at both $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent) and $\alpha{=}1.0$, but 0/8 through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
30	The transition zone at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$ is where method divergence is most dangerous: correlation-based methods find significance across all levels while causal methods remain null through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$, FDR $p{=}0.053$, but does not reach aggregate detection), creating the maximum risk of spurious conclusions when only a single (liberal) method is used.
31	This regime dependence is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short ecological time series \cite{boettiger2012limits}, and suggests that detectability boundaries should be explicitly mapped rather than assumed.
32	
33	
34	\subsection{Multi-Method Consensus Framework}
35	\label{sec:consensus}
36	
37	The pitfalls above motivate a multi-method consensus approach inspired by specification curve analysis \cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method validation in early-warning signal detection \cite{scheffer2009early}: rather than relying on any single method, we apply multiple independent methods to quantify how analytic choices determine conclusions, using agreement thresholds as diagnostic benchmarks.
38	
39	\paragraph{Formal definition.}
40	Given $M$ lead-lag detection methods $\{m_1, \ldots, m_M\}$ and $N$ independent random seeds, a canary$\to$downstream pair $(X, Y)$ is classified as \textsc{robust} if and only if:
41	\begin{enumerate}
42	    \item At least $K$ of $M$ methods judge the pair FDR-significant, where each method independently applies Benjamini--Hochberg correction at $q{=}0.05$; and
43	    \item At least $S$ of $N$ seeds replicate this conclusion.
44	\end{enumerate}
45	The thresholds $(K, S)$ control the trade-off between false positive and false negative rates.
46	Methods with different inductive biases (correlation-based methods that detect any temporal association versus Granger-type methods that test directional predictive improvement \cite{granger1969investigating}) provide complementary evidence.
47	Their convergence on a given pair constitutes stronger evidence than agreement among methods sharing the same statistical assumptions.
48	We note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality \cite{shojaie2022granger}; our framework inherits this limitation.
49	
50	\paragraph{Method tiering.}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
5	Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
6	As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
7	By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
8	This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
9	The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.
10	Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators, and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
11	
12	Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
13	Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation---or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
14	Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
15	In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
16	This makes both the validity and the regime-dependence of existing canary claims open questions with direct consequences for practitioners who rely on such signals to trigger training interventions.
17	
18	We identify four specific deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
19	(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends, a well-documented hazard in analyses of co-trending time series~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
20	(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined; no multi-method cross-validation is conducted.
21	(3)~No false discovery rate (FDR) correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg) guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
22	(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
23	The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who report that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
24	Their analysis, however, covers a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and relies on visual comparisons without statistical tests.
25	The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating} provides theoretical motivation but has not been applied to training collapse with the rigor that such short, non-stationary series require.
26	
27	We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
28	Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across eight contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$; steepness predicted T-dependent): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the boundary.
29	A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response (including a synchronous dip at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$) through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.

34	Our contributions are:
35	\begin{enumerate}
36	    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators, and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation---or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends---depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
This makes both the validity and the regime-dependence of existing canary claims open questions with direct consequences for practitioners who rely on such signals to trigger training interventions.

We identify four specific deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends, a well-documented hazard in analyses of co-trending time series~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined; no multi-method cross-validation is conducted.
(3)~No false discovery rate (FDR) correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg) guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who report that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, covers a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and relies on visual comparisons without statistical tests.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating} provides theoretical motivation but has not been applied to training collapse with the rigor that such short, non-stationary series require.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across eight contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$; steepness predicted T-dependent): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the boundary.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response (including a synchronous dip at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$) through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
The discovery is enabled by a multi-method consensus framework (MMCT)~\cite{bell2022modeling,kapoor2024reforms} comparing five statistical methods, which reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null---the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions spanning the full spectrum.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$ generations, canary-downstream causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, steepness $k{\geq}200$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$; steepness predicted T-dependent by power theory, Contribution~2): PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (dual-seed), despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the boundary.
    A non-monotonic dose-response establishes a four-regime structure: \emph{blind} ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$, PermG 0/8; sub-threshold signal present, see Contribution~2), \emph{onset} ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha{\approx}0.60$, 0--3/8, dual-seed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed, three seeds; 6/8 at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).
    The detection threshold is governed by per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha$, not cumulative contamination.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed (distinct-1 drops 39.6\%) but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null (entropy drift $-5.3\%$ vs.\ null $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%), with directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) confirmed across four seeds on WikiText-103.

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution theory} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A $S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha)$ framework predicts the non-monotonic dose-response: signal strength $S$ increases monotonically with $\alpha$, but temporal resolution $R$ drops at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$ when relaxation time matches the observation interval.
    A statistical power interpretation formalizes the onset as a power threshold---$\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma\bigr)$---generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$: left-shift of $\alpha_c$, transition smoothing, and method-dependent detection thresholds.
    Empirical validation of prediction~(iii) awaits $T{=}20$ replication; at $T{=}10$, sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ (FDR $p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}, \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
    The Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT), comparing five lead-lag methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, serves as the instrument enabling the above discovery.
    It exposes three methodological pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\% (inter-method $\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 20/24 FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.
    PermG emerges as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with high sensitivity, identifying token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection and cessation} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    Predictive cessation (triggered when token entropy drops ${>}15\%$) fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation, reducing peak perplexity by 58\% (pooled estimate; bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%)\footnote{Bootstrap CI computed from two seed-precision pairs (s42 fp32, s43 bf16); the interval reflects observed variation rather than population-level uncertainty.} and enabling convergence one generation faster.
    A four-layer detection taxonomy---dimensionality collapse ($\alpha{\geq}0.10$), distributional variance ($\alpha{\geq}0.25$), causal coupling ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$), dynamical stability ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$)---provides practitioners with regime-appropriate diagnostic tools.
    Results are validated across two model scales (Pythia-410M, Pythia-1.4B), confirming scale-independent trigger and recovery patterns.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}), cross-architecture generalization (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), and canary-based early intervention (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and future directions, and \S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

50	\paragraph{Method tiering.}
51	The five methods are organized into two tiers based on empirical reliability.
52	Three \emph{primary} methods---naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, and permutation Granger causality---produce consistent results across independent analysis pipelines and exhibit adequate statistical power at $T{=}11$ generations.
53	Two methods are classified as \emph{supplementary}: threshold onset detection due to power limitations at $T{=}11$ under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality, which achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) but with reduced power relative to the primary methods (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
54	The consensus panel thus comprises four contributing methods (three primary, one moderate supplementary), with threshold onset near-inoperative at $T{=}11$.
55	The consensus threshold $K{\geq}3$ out of 5 methods requires agreement among at least the three primary methods or two primary methods plus TY, making $K{\geq}3$ a \emph{stronger} standard than a simple majority vote would suggest.
56	
57	\paragraph{Sequential filtering pipeline.}
58	In practice, the $K$-of-$M$ voting operates over all five methods applied independently to each pair; the sequential pipeline below describes the order in which results are examined, enabling early termination and interpretable diagnostics at each stage (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}):
59	\begin{enumerate}
60	    \item \textbf{Naive correlation scan.} Cross-correlation at maximum lag~5 with BH correction serves as a permissive baseline; all pairs with any temporal association pass.
61	    \item \textbf{First-differencing diagnostic.} Cross-correlation is recomputed on first-differenced series, testing whether temporal associations survive removal of shared linear trends. Pairs that lose significance are flagged as potential spurious regressions.
62	    \item \textbf{Permutation Granger causality.} Permutation-based Granger causality tests \cite{shojaie2022granger} on first-differenced series (5{,}000 permutations, BH correction at $q{=}0.05$) assess directional predictive improvement: whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history.
63	    \item \textbf{Multi-seed replication.} The conclusion must hold across $S$ of $N$ independent training seeds, filtering seed-specific artifacts.
64	\end{enumerate}
65	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this pipeline progressively filters: 16 pairs pass Stage~1, 14 survive Stage~2 (differencing removes 2 marginal canary$\to$perplexity pairs), 6 survive Stage~3 (Granger testing eliminates remaining canary$\to$perplexity pairs and failed canary candidates), and all~6 survive Stage~4 (multi-seed replication confirms all Granger-significant pairs).
66	
67	\begin{figure}[t]
68	\centering
69	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/consensus_workflow.pdf}
70	\caption{Sequential filtering pipeline of the multi-method consensus framework. Starting from all candidate canary$\to$downstream pairs, the pipeline applies four stages: (1)~naive cross-correlation scan (permissive baseline), (2)~first-differencing diagnostic (removes shared-trend artifacts), (3)~permutation Granger causality (tests directional predictive improvement), and (4)~multi-seed replication (filters seed-specific artifacts). At $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M), the pipeline reduces 16 candidate pairs to 6 robust pairs: 16$\to$14$\to$6$\to$6. The $K$-of-$M$ consensus vote operates in parallel across all five methods; the sequential ordering provides interpretable diagnostics at each stage.}
71	\label{fig:consensus_workflow}
72	\end{figure}
73	
74	\paragraph{Practical guidance.}
75	The consensus thresholds $(K, S)$ should be chosen to match the analyst's tolerance for false positives versus false negatives.
76	Table~\ref{tab:practical_guidance} provides four recommended tiers, calibrated against our experimental controls (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
77	Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$, $S{\geq}3/4$) achieves the best trade-off under the full 5-method panel: zero false positives while recovering all six reference pairs; however, threshold onset's near-zero power at $3\sigma$ (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}) makes it near-inoperative, and Toda--Yamamoto provides moderate supplementary signal (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), making $K{\geq}3$ the operationally relevant consensus threshold.
78	With four contributing methods (three primary plus TY), $K{\geq}3$ draws on a broader evidence base than the three primary methods alone; TY's moderate detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ strengthens consensus conclusions where it contributes a positive vote.
79	Cross-architecture validation confirms $K{\geq}3$ reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 architecture-seed combinations (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
80	Method subset ablation confirms that this threshold is uniquely optimal: at $K{=}3/5$, the null-control FPR is 37.5\% (unacceptable); at $K{=}4/5$, FPR drops to 0\% while retaining 6/6 reference-pair sensitivity; at $K{=}5/5$, FPR remains 0\% but sensitivity falls to 3/6.
81	Shapley value analysis (exact enumeration of all 32 coalitions; Figure~\ref{fig:shapley}) identifies naive cross-correlation as the sole positive contributor to FPR (Shapley(FPR)${=}{+}0.348$) and permutation Granger as the strongest FPR suppressor (Shapley(FPR)${=}{-}0.194$), the only method combining 0\% null-control FPR with high sensitivity.
82	Toda--Yamamoto's Shapley contribution (FNR${=}{-}0.158$) reflects moderate supplementary value: it reduces consensus FNR without introducing false positives (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
83	
84	\begin{figure}[t]
85	\centering
86	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/shapley_method_contribution.pdf}
87	\caption{Shapley value decomposition of method contributions to consensus FPR and FNR (exact enumeration of all $2^5{=}32$ coalitions, $K{=}\max(1,|S|{-}1)$). FPR is computed at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (3~seeds $\times$ 8~pairs${=}$24 observations); FNR at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4~seeds, 6 reference pairs). Naive cross-correlation is the only positive FPR contributor (${+}0.348$); permutation Granger is the strongest FPR suppressor (${-}0.194$). Toda--Yamamoto contributes moderate FNR suppression (Shapley FNR${=}{-}0.158$) as a supplementary method (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).}
88	\label{fig:shapley}
89	\end{figure}
90	Tier~4 requires unanimity across methods and seeds, which incurs elevated false negative rates; TY's moderate detection (3--4/8) means that requiring $5/5$ unanimity is substantially more restrictive than $4/5$, particularly at intermediate contamination levels where TY may not contribute a positive vote.

145	This low power is expected: with only 10 generation-over-generation differences, the null variance estimate has few degrees of freedom, and a $3\sigma$ exceedance threshold becomes overly conservative.
146	We retain threshold onset as a supplementary method for completeness and report its results transparently, but adopt permutation Granger forward significance as the primary detection indicator in cross-architecture analyses.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
$K{\geq}3$ multi-method consensus reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 conditions with known consensus (Padding-410M and Pythia-1.4B C4 pending audit), confirming that multi-method agreement generalizes beyond the calibration setup; Pythia-1.4B (s42: 1/8, s43: 3/8) and SmolLM3-3B (3/8) reflect scale-dependent seed sensitivity and canary metric splitting rather than framework failure.
Reverse-direction tests at $\alpha{=}1.0$ reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence at full synthetic replacement), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
The unidirectionality of token entropy is domain-dependent: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4 (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling absent from all WikiText conditions at any contamination level (see below).
GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance, placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (consistent with the null regime) and moderate detection (3--4/8) only at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to method recommendation.}
The primary value of the multi-method framework is not the consensus vote itself but the systematic comparison it enables.
By applying five methods with different inductive biases to the same data, the framework reveals \emph{why} each method succeeds or fails: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR because it captures reverse-directional associations; differenced cross-correlation cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence; threshold onset lacks power at $T{=}11$ under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}); and Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8) but remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
This process of elimination converges on permutation Granger as the recommended method: it is the only one combining zero null-control FPR, consistent detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$, and clean directional separation on WikiText (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution, maintaining FPR${=}$0\%; however, the practical recommendation is simpler: for short iterative training series, permutation Granger alone provides reliable detection without requiring the full consensus machinery.
Multi-method consensus ($K{\geq}3$) remains useful as a robustness check, reaching ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 cross-architecture conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), but threshold onset is power-limited and Toda--Yamamoto provides moderate supplementary signal (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with four contributing methods supporting the $K{\geq}3$ threshold.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
After correcting a statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), confirming that its lower rates reflect genuine power limitations at $T{=}11$ rather than implementation error.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
After implementation correction, Toda--Yamamoto's window sensitivity is consistent with its moderate detection profile: TY consensus stabilizes at $T{\geq}6$, slightly later than the primary methods ($T{\geq}5$), reflecting the additional degrees of freedom consumed by the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{Four-layer detection taxonomy.}
Our results suggest a layered taxonomy for detecting iterative training degradation, ordered by onset threshold:
(1)~\emph{Distributional dimensionality} (effective rank): detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom, with onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.10$ (established);
(2)~\emph{Distributional instability} (entropy variance): detects inflated fluctuations in canary metrics across generations, with suggestive onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$ (a $10\times$ variance inflation from $0.004$ to $0.04$), well before causal coupling emerges;
(3)~\emph{Causal coupling} (Granger-type tests): detects temporal precedence between canary and downstream metrics, with onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ (the detection phase transition established in \S\ref{sec:regime}); and
(4)~\emph{Dynamical stability} (AC1): suggestive evidence of autocorrelation shifts near the onset boundary (see below), but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$.
Layers~1 and~3 are established; Layers~2 and~4 are suggestive and require longer generation protocols for confirmation ($T{\geq}50$; \citealt{dakos2012methods}).

55	\paragraph{Suggestive CSD signatures.}
56	Exploratory analysis reveals a CSD-consistent pattern: canary metrics show rising autocorrelation (Kendall $\tau{=}0.79$--$0.82$, $p{<}0.001$) while downstream diversity metrics show none ($\tau{=}0.03$--$0.30$, $p{>}0.19$), suggestive of a temporal sequence in which canary destabilization precedes downstream collapse.

63	In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.

65	The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
66	This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines---a limitation specific to the dimensionality layer that does not affect the causal coupling layer (Granger detectability), which remains consistent across architectures.

68	\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
69	Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
70	Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).

73	\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}

99	\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
100	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.

105	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
